sections.section: Structural and Kinematic Evolution at Cosmic Noon

claims.text: Cosmic noon (z approximately 2, lookback time approximately 10 Gyr) is the peak era of cosmic star formation and the major assembly epoch of present-day massive galaxies, integrating scaling relations, gas reservoirs, resolved kinematics, and outflows into a regulated equilibrium-growth picture (accretion, star formation, feedback, recycling).

Ionized-gas velocity dispersions in rotation-dominated massive disks are elevated at high redshift and decline toward lower redshift (intrinsic sigma_0 approximately 50 km/s at z approximately 2.3 falling to approximately 25 km/s at z approximately 0.9 in KMOS3D), consistent with marginally gravitationally stable disks near Toomre Q approximately 1.

At fixed stellar mass, star-forming galaxies are smaller at higher redshift, with rest-optical effective radius scaling approximately as R_eff proportional to (1+z)^-0.75 for late types and about (1+z)^-1.48 for quiescent galaxies over 0 < z < 3.
Massive main-sequence galaxies at z approximately 1-3 contain large molecular-gas reservoirs with molecular depletion times of order 0.7-1.0 Gyr, markedly shorter than local disks.

In dynamical models the inner regions (within roughly one effective radius) of many massive cosmic-noon disks are baryon-dominated, with low inferred central dark-matter fractions (median f_DM(<R_eff) approximately 8% for a Chabrier IMF in the MOSDEF z approximately 2 sample) and falling outer rotation curves.

Broad ionized-gas components reveal galaxy-scale outflows in normal (non-AGN) star-forming galaxies across z = 0.6-2.7, establishing feedback-driven outflows as a common feature of the cosmic-noon main-sequence population.

Bulge growth, dense central cores, and compact star-forming systems are observationally linked to pathways toward quiescence, connecting compact star-forming galaxies to compact quiescent descendants.

Whether the star-forming main sequence is near-linear or bent/high-mass-flattened, and how its slope and normalization evolve with redshift, remains unresolved because SFR indicators, dust corrections, IMF, selection, stacking, and bulge contamination shift the fits.
claims.debate_topic: Main-sequence slope and normalization at cosmic noon

claims.text: Whether the cosmic-noon massive population is best described as predominantly ordered rotating disks or as retaining a major dynamically disturbed/merging fraction is unresolved, since resolution, depth, kinematic classification, pair timescales, and selection prevent a universal fraction.
claims.debate_topic: Disks versus mergers among massive cosmic-noon galaxies

claims.text: Whether giant kiloparsec-scale clumps are long-lived bound structures that migrate inward to build bulges or are short-lived features rapidly disrupted by stellar feedback is contested, as inferred clump ages, masses, and gradients are resolution- and model-dependent and simulations differ in feedback strength.

Whether the low inferred inner dark-matter fractions of cosmic-noon disks reflect genuine baryon dominance or are an artifact of pressure support, IMF and gas-mass assumptions, halo contraction versus cored profiles, and sample selection is unresolved, and low central dark matter does not imply the absence of a dark halo.
claims.debate_topic: Origin of low inner dark-matter fractions at cosmic noon

claims.text: Whether massive galaxies evolve through central compaction before quenching or through gradual inside-out disk growth with bulge buildup is unresolved, because cross-sectional populations do not uniquely reconstruct evolutionary tracks and resolved SEDs are dust- and model-sensitive.

sections.section: Stellar Population Synthesis and Stellar-Mass Systematics

claims.text: A stellar population synthesis prediction combines an IMF, stellar-evolution isochrones, and stellar spectra into simple stellar populations, then convolves these with a star-formation history, chemical enrichment, and dust to build composite populations, so every SED-inferred galaxy property inherits the adopted ingredients and priors.

Stellar mass is among the more robust SED-derived galaxy properties but remains a model-dependent stellar mass-to-light scaling rather than a direct observation, sensitive to the IMF and to hidden old populations.

The statistical uncertainty on normal-SFH stellar masses is of order 0.3 dex, but assumed star-formation-history flexibility can shift recovered mass, age, and past SFR by up to about 0.6 dex in extreme cases because young stars outshine older mass.

Old-population optical colors and many absorption indices suffer a strong age-metallicity degeneracy (the Worthey 3/2 rule: an age change of a factor about 3 mimics a metallicity change of a factor about 2), most severe for populations older than about 5 Gyr and reducible but not erasable with high-S/N full spectra (S/N greater than about 100 per Angstrom).

The treatment of thermally-pulsing asymptotic-giant-branch (TP-AGB) stars drives large near-infrared SPS differences for intermediate-age populations (roughly 0.1-2 Gyr), whereas optical color-based mass-to-light estimates are generally less sensitive to the TP-AGB prescription than near-infrared estimates.

The low-mass IMF normalization strongly controls stellar mass-to-light ratios while contributing little integrated light, so that roughly 60-80% of the stellar mass of an old population can reside in low-mass stars that add little optical or near-infrared luminosity.

By 2013 gravity-sensitive absorption spectra, dynamical modeling, and strong lensing had provided independent evidence that massive early-type galaxies may have heavier IMF normalizations than the Milky Way, though abundance responses, dark matter, and dynamical degeneracies remain.

Extinction and attenuation laws are not universal or interchangeable because geometry and stellar age alter effective attenuation; panchromatic energy-balance models can nonetheless connect attenuated UV-optical starlight to infrared dust emission when UV-to-IR coverage is available.

Nebular emission lines and continuum can materially contaminate the broadband SEDs of high-equivalent-width galaxies and bias inferred stellar parameters if omitted, strongest for high-sSFR, low-metallicity, high-redshift systems; empirical and theoretical stellar libraries also carry complementary limitations in parameter and abundance coverage.

Whether TP-AGB stars contribute strongly or weakly to the intermediate-age near-infrared light is unresolved, because cluster calibrators, stochasticity, metallicity, SFH, and circumstellar dust permit competing fits (TP-AGB-heavy versus lighter models).

Whether the stellar IMF is universal (Milky-Way-like) or varies systematically with velocity dispersion or abundance is unresolved, since spectral features, dynamics, lensing, abundance patterns, remnants, and dark matter are mutually degenerate; because the IMF sets absolute stellar masses it propagates into both the star-forming main sequence normalization and the stellar-to-halo mass relation.

Whether star-formation histories are best modeled with simple parametric (exponential or rising) forms or with nonparametric, burst-capable reconstructions is contested, since flexible models reduce bias but increase prior dependence and time-bin covariance.

Whether absolute stellar masses are accurate at the factor-of-two level or carry substantially larger SPS, IMF, and SFH systematics is debated, because formal fit errors omit model mismatch and unseen low-mass or old populations.

Whether UV, recombination-line (Halpha), IR, and full-SED star-formation rates should agree is unresolved for bursty or dusty populations, since each tracer weights different stellar ages (UV averaging about 100 Myr, Halpha less than about 10 Myr) and different dust-heating sources.

The central-galaxy stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR) is strongly non-linear, with maximum integrated galaxy-formation efficiency near a Milky-Way-scale halo (pivot M_h approximately 10^12 M_sun) where the integrated efficiency M*/(f_b M_h) remains below about 20% (approximately 0.15-0.20) at z approximately 0.

The intrinsic scatter in central stellar mass at fixed halo mass above the pivot is small, generally below about 0.2 dex (approximately 0.16-0.20 dex), usually assumed lognormal and inferred jointly from abundance, clustering, and lensing after measurement errors are removed.

Below the pivot, central stellar mass falls steeply with decreasing halo mass and the slope and scatter become increasingly uncertain toward dwarfs, where incompleteness, reionization, stellar-mass estimates, stripping, and central-versus-satellite definitions dominate.

At group and cluster masses the central stellar mass grows much more slowly than halo mass (roughly M*_central proportional to M_h^(1/3)), once brightest-cluster-galaxy photometry, intracluster light, and central-versus-total stellar mass are distinguished.

Halo occupation distribution (HOD) and conditional luminosity function (CLF) models require separate central and satellite occupation distributions to reproduce galaxy abundance and scale-dependent clustering, with the satellite occupation following a near-power-law set by the subhalo mass function.

Subhalo abundance matching reproduces galaxy abundance and clustering by rank-ordering galaxies and halos/subhalos using a chosen proxy with scatter, forming a robust empirical framework underpinned by N-body-calibrated halo mass functions and bias relations.

The one-halo/two-halo transition produces measurable departures from a single power law in galaxy clustering, and galaxy-galaxy lensing combined with clustering provides complementary constraints on mean halo mass, satellite fraction, and occupation.

Dark-matter halo clustering depends on formation history and concentration at fixed halo mass (halo assembly bias) in collisionless simulations, with amplitude and sign depending on halo mass, secondary property, environment, and halo finder.

Satellite galaxies have systematically different star formation and colors from comparable centrals, and infall histories imply delayed-then-rapid quenching for local satellites (delay of about 2-4 Gyr followed by a rapid e-folding of less than about 0.8 Gyr for M* greater than 5e9 M_sun).

Whether galaxy occupation depends only on halo mass or must explicitly couple galaxy properties to halo formation history or concentration (galaxy assembly bias) is unresolved, since halo masses and secondary properties are noisy and correlated and environment can mimic the signal.

The dominant origin of intrinsic SHMR scatter is contested among merger/accretion history, concentration, spin, baryonic stochasticity, and residual measurement error, because inferred intrinsic scatter depends on deconvolution and on cross-correlated galaxy observables (including the SPS-driven stellar-mass systematics).

The optimal abundance-matching proxy is unresolved among present Vmax or M, peak velocity or mass, infall values, and compound concentration-sensitive proxies, because satellite stripping and disruption, resolution, and orphan galaxies change small-scale clustering.

The dominant satellite-quenching mechanism is unresolved among starvation/strangulation, ram-pressure stripping, tidal effects, and preprocessing, because demographics constrain delay and fade times better than they isolate a unique physical mechanism.

Halo-mass inference is method-dependent: clustering/HOD, abundance, group catalogs, weak lensing, satellite dynamics, X-ray, and SZ constraints carry different degeneracies, and dark-matter-only halo statistics may require baryonic corrections (contraction, expansion, redistribution) at survey precision, so no method recovers a model-free halo mass.
